newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa seeks to bar mercenary actions abroad.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa seeks to bar mercenary actions abroad.

text.p: South Africa's cabinet said on Wednesday it would rush through legislation barring unauthorised mercenary activity abroad with a penalty of up to 10 years or a fine of one million rand ($225,000).

Kader Asmal, a cabinet minister in President Nelson Mandela's government who heads the country's arms policy grouping, told a news conference that he would also request other countries implement similar laws.

"We are pioneering the legislation. No country has yet introduced such a comprehensive piece of legislation...It is of far-reaching importance, because I'm going to ask other countries to copy our legislation," Asmal said.

Companies and individuals wanting to offer any military- related services abroad -- the best-known is Pretoria-based Executive Outcomes -- must in future seek government approval and receive the authorisation before entering into contracts.

South African courts will be given the jurisdiction to enforce the law, regardless of where an offence is committed. Asmal said a public register would be drawn up, and even universities offering advice abroad were not exempt.
Mandela's government has repeatedly been embarrassed at reports of South African mercenary activity abroad.

Reports last month said South African soldiers of fortune were on standby to help Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko hold the capital Kinshasa from rebels, and that another group of mercenaries was alleged to be working in Zaire alongside Ugandan troops loyal to Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila.

South African mercenaries hired by Papua New Guinea to put down an island rebellion with the British-based Sandline International returned home last month, after being expelled by the soldiers they were meant to have helped.
"We'll be putting them on notice," Asmal said, referring to companies already active abroad.
The pending legislation would be "fast-tracked" through parliament and was due to be tabled within weeks, he added.

The government is given the right to veto any military activity if the deal may result in the suppression of human rights, destabilise a region, prejudice South Africa's interests or if the country involved supports terrorism.
"If it violates this 'nyet' -- no," Asmal said. But he said that permission would not necessarily be extremely difficult to obtain and quipped:
"Every country in the world has skeletons in the cupboard. What we are talking about is -- is there a graveyard?"
